title: Artificial_psychology
summary:
Artificial psychology has had multiple meanings dating back to the 19th century, with recent usage related to artificial intelligence. In 1999, Zhiliang Wang and Lun Xie presented a theory of artificial psychology based on artificial intelligence. They analyze human psychology using information science research methods and artificial intelligence research to probe deeper into the human mind.

Dan Curtis proposed that artificial psychology is a theoretical discipline. The theory considers the situation when an artificial intelligence approaches the level of complexity where it is capable of reprogramming itself based on new data, allowing it to evolve, and is capable of resolving its own programming conflicts even in the presence of incomplete data, meaning the intelligence autonomously makes value-based decisions referring to values it has created for itself.

When both conditions are met, the possibility exists that the intelligence will reach irrational conclusions. At this point, intervention may not be resolved by simple re-coding due to the extraordinarily complex nature of the codebase, but rather requires a discussion with the intelligence resembling classical human psychology. If the intelligence requires itself to reprogram through analysis and decision based on information provided by a human to overcome dysfunctional behavior, then artificial psychology is, by definition, what is required.

The level of complexity required before these thresholds are met is currently a subject of extensive debate. Artificial psychology does not address the question of whether or not the intelligence is conscious. As of 2022, the level of artificial intelligence does not approach any threshold where the theories or principles of artificial psychology can even be tested, and therefore artificial psychology remains a largely theoretical discipline. The attempt to understand and engineer these abilities constitutes the new interdisciplinary field of artificial psychology, characterized by contributions from philosophy, cognitive psychology, neuroscience, computer science, and robotics.
